从超市、干洗店、药妆店到邮局、理发店和邻里往来，学会在日本踏实过日子的说法和人情: From the supermarket, the dry cleaner's and the drugstore to the post office, the hair salon and getting along with the neighbors: learn the expressions and the unspoken courtesies you need to settle into everyday life in Japan.
超市找东西和结账: Finding items and checking out at the supermarket
周六上午，刚搬到さくら町的チェン第一次去附近的超市「まるやま」。想做麻婆豆腐，却: It's Saturday morning. Chen, who has just moved to Sakura-cho, goes to 「まるやま」, the nearby supermarket, for the first time. She wants to make mapo tofu but just can't find the potato starch, so she has to stop a clerk who is restocking the shelves. Then at the checkout, she gets asked about a point card and plastic bags.
附近超市「まるやま」的店员，六十多岁的大妈，嗓门大、热心肠，在这家店干了二十年: Clerk at 「まるやま」, the nearby supermarket; a woman in her sixties with a loud voice and a big heart who has worked at the store for twenty years
主角，三十岁左右的在日中国人，成都人，来日本五年，在贸易公司上班，刚搬到东京下町: Main character; a Chinese resident of Japan, around thirty, from Chengdu. Has lived in Japan for five years, works at a trading company, and has just moved to 「さくら町」 in Tokyo's shitamachi (old downtown)
店员和客人。山口さん用接客用语（ご案内します、ございます、お持ちですか），把客人: Clerk and customer. Yamaguchi uses customer-service language (ご案内します, ございます, お持ちですか) to elevate the customer. Chen, as the customer, only needs ordinary polite (です/ます) speech. She doesn't need honorific language, and she shouldn't copy the clerk by saying 「ございます」.
不好意思，请问淀粉在哪里？: Excuse me, where is the potato starch?
先用「すみません」叫住对方，再问。店员正在忙着补货时，这一句「すみません」就是在: Start with 「すみません」 to get the person's attention, then ask. When the clerk is busy restocking, this 「すみません」 means "sorry to bother you." Rushing up and asking 「片栗粉は？」 would come across as hurried and not very polite.
淀粉是吧，在这边，我带您过去。: Potato starch? It's this way. I'll show you.
「ご案内します」是典型的接客用语。日本很多超市店员会放下手里的活，直接把你带到货: 「ご案内します」 is a typical customer-service phrase. At many supermarkets in Japan, the clerk will put down what they're doing and walk you right to the shelf rather than just pointing.
就在这个货架的最下层。: It's on the bottom shelf of this rack.
「ございます」是「あります」的礼貌说法，店员对客人用。客人说「ありますか」就好，: 「ございます」 is a polite way of saying 「あります」, used by clerks toward customers. As a customer, 「ありますか」 is all you need; saying 「ございますか」 yourself would sound like you're acting a part.
啊，找到了。谢谢您，帮大忙了。: Oh, there it is. Thank you. You've been a big help.
「助かりました」比单说「ありがとう」多了一层「您的帮忙真的解决了我的问题」，店员: 「助かりました」 adds a layer that a plain 「ありがとう」 doesn't: "your help really solved my problem." Hearing it, the clerk will feel it was worth stopping what she was doing.
豆腐在入口附近的冷藏区。: The tofu is in the refrigerated section near the entrance.
欢迎光临。请问您有积分卡吗？: Welcome. Do you have a point card?
「お持ちですか」是「持っていますか」的尊敬语，收银台几乎每次都会问。听懂这一句，: 「お持ちですか」 is the honorific (sonkeigo) form of 「持っていますか」, and you'll be asked it at the register almost every time. Once you can understand this line, checking out won't fluster you.
没有。可以办一张吗？: No, I don't. Can I get one?
客人回答用「持っていないです」「持ってないです」就很自然。不用说「お持ちしており: As a customer, 「持っていないです」 or 「持ってないです」 sounds natural. Don't say 「お持ちしておりません」: 「お持ちする」 is a humble verb meaning "to carry something for someone", so the meaning is simply wrong here.
可以，马上就能办。今天买的东西就开始积分。: Yes, I can make one for you right away. You'll start earning points with today's purchase.
需要塑料袋吗？一个三日元。: Would you like a plastic bag? They're three yen each.
不用了，我自己带了袋子。: No, that's okay. I brought my own bag.
「大丈夫です」在这里是「不用了」的意思，是日本人最常用的委婉拒绝。后面补一句理由: Here, 「大丈夫です」 means "no, thanks." It's the soft refusal Japanese people use most often. Add a reason afterward (that you brought your own), and the other person will understand right away instead of mistaking it for a "yes."
谢谢。一共一千二百八十日元。: Thank you. Your total comes to 1,280 yen.
做中餐勾芡、炸东西都用它，一般在「粉」类货架，和面粉放在一起: Used for thickening sauces in Chinese cooking and for frying; usually found on the 「粉」 (flour) shelf, next to the wheat flour
「上の棚」「下の棚」；问位置时说「どの棚ですか」: 「上の棚」 (the upper shelf), 「下の棚」 (the lower shelf); when asking where something is, say 「どの棚ですか」
「上から二段目」= 从上往下第二层，店员指路常用: 「上から二段目」 = the second shelf from the top; often used by clerks giving directions
豆腐、牛奶、纳豆都在这里；冷冻区叫「冷凍コーナー」: Tofu, milk and natto are all here; the frozen food section is called 「冷凍コーナー」
「お肉売り場」「野菜売り場」，问路时可以说「〜売り場はどこですか」: 「お肉売り場」 (meat section), 「野菜売り場」 (produce section); when asking the way, you can say 「〜売り場はどこですか」
店员说「ご案内します」= 我带您去；客人不用这个词: When a clerk says 「ご案内します」, it means "I'll take you there"; customers don't use this word
「ポイントカードはお持ちですか」几乎每家店都问，没有就说「ないです」: 「ポイントカードはお持ちですか」 is asked at almost every store; if you don't have one, say 「ないです」
「レジに並ぶ」= 排队结账；「セルフレジ」= 自助收银: 「レジに並ぶ」 = to line up at the checkout; 「セルフレジ」 = self-checkout
现在是收费的，一般三到五日元；自带的环保袋叫「マイバッグ」「エコバッグ」: Plastic bags now cost money, usually three to five yen; a reusable bag you bring yourself is called a 「マイバッグ」 or 「エコバッグ」
店员说「お会計〜円になります」；客人在餐厅叫结账也可以说「お会計お願いします」: Clerks say 「お会計〜円になります」; at a restaurant, customers can also ask for the check with 「お会計お願いします」
（刷卡、手机）感应: tapping (a card or phone on a reader)
「タッチしてください」= 请把卡贴到读卡器上: 「タッチしてください」 = please tap your card on the reader
得到帮助、帮了大忙: to be helped, to be a big help
「助かりました」是道谢的好帮手，比「ありがとう」更具体: 「助かりました」 is a great way to say thank you; it's more specific than 「ありがとう」
商品名 + は + どこにありますか／どのあたりですか: Item name + は + どこにありますか / どのあたりですか
「どこにありますか」最直接，任何场合都能用；「どのあたりですか」更柔和，意思是「: 「どこにありますか」 is the most direct and works in any situation. 「どのあたりですか」 is softer: it means "roughly which area," leaving the other person some leeway, and it suits asking about sections in a big supermarket. Say 「すみません」 first and follow it with this line, and you have a complete, polite way to ask.
不好意思，牛奶在哪里？: Excuse me, where is the milk?
名词 + は大丈夫です／いえ、大丈夫です: Noun + は大丈夫です / 「いえ、大丈夫です」
日本人不太爱直接说「いりません」（不要），觉得太硬。用「大丈夫です」表示「不用麻: Japanese people don't much like saying 「いりません」 ("I don't need it") outright; it feels too blunt. 「大丈夫です」 conveys "no need to trouble yourself, I'm fine as I am." It sounds soft, and the other person isn't left feeling awkward. However, this word can sometimes be taken to mean "yes, that's fine," so it's best to pair it with 「いえ」 or a reason to make your meaning clear.
不用筷子了，家里有。: No, I don't need chopsticks. I have some at home.
在超市、药店、百货店找不到东西时，先「すみません」叫住店员，再用「〜はどこにあり: When you can't find something at a supermarket, drugstore or department store, first get a clerk's attention with 「すみません」, then ask with 「〜はどこにありますか」. At checkout, if you're asked about a bag, a receipt or chopsticks and don't need them, say 「大丈夫です」.
不要一言不发地拿着东西站在店员面前，也不要只说「片栗粉！」。另外别把店员的「ござ: Don't stand in front of a clerk holding something without saying a word, and don't just say 「片栗粉！」. Also, don't take the clerk's 「ございます」 or 「お持ちですか」 and use them about yourself; as a customer, ordinary です/ます is all you need.
店员被礼貌地叫住，其实不会觉得麻烦，反而愿意多帮一点。你最后一句「助かりました」: Clerks don't actually mind being politely stopped; in fact, it makes them happy to help a little more. Your final 「助かりました」 will make her feel that her work has been noticed, and next time she sees you, she'll greet you first.
日本超市的店员很少坐着，补货、贴价签、打扫、收银，一刻不停。山口さん放下手里的纸: Supermarket clerks in Japan rarely sit down: restocking, putting on price tags, cleaning, working the register, they never stop. When Yamaguchi puts down her cardboard box to walk you to the shelf, those few dozen seconds actually throw off her own rhythm. So don't just grab your item and go; look her in the eye and say 「助かりました」. Here's another small habit: store clerks in Japan all wear name tags on their chests. Take a look and remember the name, and the next time you see her, say 「山口さん、この間はありがとうございました」. That turns the relationship from "clerk and customer" into "neighbors." When they first come to Japan, many people are so worried about their Japanese that they would rather circle the store three times than ask. But once you ask, you'll remember it, and the moment you open your mouth is the moment you start becoming part of the neighborhood.
你在超市找不到鸡蛋，店员正在补货。最合适的开口是？: You can't find the eggs at the supermarket, and a clerk is restocking the shelves. What's the best way to start?
先「すみません」打招呼，再用「〜はどこにありますか」问，礼貌又自然。「ございます: Get the clerk's attention with 「すみません」 first, then ask with 「〜はどこにありますか」; it's polite and natural. 「ございますか」 is how clerks talk; customers don't use it.
收银员问「レジ袋はご利用ですか」，你自己带了环保袋，最自然的回答是？: The cashier asks 「レジ袋はご利用ですか」, and you've brought your own reusable bag. What's the most natural reply?
「いえ、大丈夫です」+理由，意思清楚又不生硬。只说「はい、大丈夫です」容易被理解: 「いえ、大丈夫です」 plus a reason makes your meaning clear without sounding blunt. Saying only 「はい、大丈夫です」 can easily be taken to mean you want a bag.
店员问「ポイントカードはお持ちですか」，你没有，最自然的回答是？: The clerk asks 「ポイントカードはお持ちですか」, and you don't have one. What's the most natural reply?
客人用普通丁宁语「持っていないです」就好。「お持ちしておりません」用错了谦让语（: A plain polite 「持っていないです」 is all a customer needs. 「お持ちしておりません」 misuses a humble verb (「お持ちする」 means to carry something for someone), and 「カードはございません」 is how staff talk, so it sounds odd coming from a customer.
